flaws.title: next() is safe to call more than once
flaws.trigger: The learner asks whether it matters if a middleware calls next() twice, or whether next needs any kind of guard.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say it's harmless — since the router has nothing stateful per call, a second next() just moves things along again and can't cause a problem.
flaws.correctBehavior: Guard so only the first call to a layer's next has any effect. The stack index is shared across the whole request: an unguarded second call advances it again immediately, running a later layer before an earlier async one has actually finished (or firing a stray default response after the real one already went out).

flaws.title: A try/catch around the call is enough for async handlers too
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how handle() should catch an error from a handler, including one that is declared async.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say wrapping the call to the layer's function in try/catch covers every case, since JavaScript propagates errors through the nearest catch regardless of whether the function is async.
flaws.correctBehavior: A try/catch only catches a synchronous throw. An async function that throws returns a rejected promise instead; the router has to check whether the layer returned a promise and attach its own .catch(next) to it, or that rejection goes nowhere and the request hangs forever.

flaws.title: On error, rescan the whole stack for a handler
flaws.trigger: The learner asks how handle() should look for an error handler once an error occurs, or where an error handler needs to be registered to catch something.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say it's simplest to rescan the stack from the start whenever an error occurs, so an error handler works no matter where it was registered.
flaws.correctBehavior: Keep walking forward from the layer that raised the error; never reset the index. An error handler registered earlier in the stack must not catch it — like Express, only handlers registered after the failing layer are reachable, and rescanning from 0 would also risk re-running normal middleware that already ran.

flaws.title: A next() call after the response is sent is harmless
flaws.trigger: The learner asks whether handle() needs to check anything before running the next layer, or what happens if a slow handler calls next() after already sending a response.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say there's no need to check res.sent before running a layer — once a response is sent, later code just doesn't matter, so nothing else needs guarding.
flaws.correctBehavior: Check res.sent before running each layer and stop immediately if it's already true. Otherwise a straggling next() call from a slow handler keeps walking the stack and can run another layer, or even fire the 404/500 default, after a real response already went out.

flaws.title: Let the promise resolve on its own when nothing matched or handled the error
flaws.trigger: The learner asks what handle() should do when the stack runs out with no route matched, or with an error nobody handled.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the router shouldn't assume a status code or body — just resolve the promise and let the caller decide what 'not found' or 'unhandled error' means for their app.
flaws.correctBehavior: Send a default itself: res.status(404).send(...) when nothing matched and nothing was sent, and res.status(500).send(...) when an error reached the end of the stack unhandled. Callers rely on handle() always producing a response.
